February: The Light Returns

February is a month of transition. Days are noticeably longer than January, and the first hints of spring appear — snowdrops, longer evenings, and the occasional mild day that has you reaching for your riding gear with renewed enthusiasm.

Conditions

  • Temperature: Average 3-8°C. Still cold, but milder spells are more frequent than January.
  • Daylight: Sunrise around 7:15am, sunset around 5pm by month's end. Significantly more riding time than January.
  • Road conditions: Still salt and grit on roads. Frost remains a morning hazard. But dry, sunny February days do occur.

February Opportunities

  • Half-term week: Roads can be quieter as families head to ski resorts. Take advantage of empty biking roads.
  • Early wildflowers: Snowdrops carpet woodland floors in February. The Cotswolds and Wye Valley are particularly beautiful.
  • Sea watching: The coast is dramatic in February. Storm-watching from a cliff-top layby (safely parked up) is a uniquely atmospheric experience.

Bike Maintenance

February is a good time for pre-season preparation:

  • Service your bike if it's been standing over winter
  • Check tyre pressures — they drop in cold weather
  • Lubricate chain and check tension
  • Charge the battery if the bike's been unused (a trickle charger over winter prevents flat batteries)
  • Clean and treat any salt corrosion from winter riding
February is the month when the riding season starts to feel possible again. Those first longer-daylight rides lift the spirits like nothing else. Even a 20-minute blast on a dry February afternoon reminds you why you ride.

Where to Ride

  • Low-level routes in the south and west offer the mildest conditions
  • Avoid mountain passes — snow and ice can persist at altitude through February
  • Coastal roads in Cornwall, Devon, and Pembrokeshire can be surprisingly pleasant

February Planning

February is prime planning time. With the touring season approaching, use the dark evenings to research routes, book accommodation for summer tours, and prepare your bike for the season ahead. Tyre manufacturers release new models in spring — February is the time to research and order if you need fresh rubber.

Many riding schools offer early-season refresher courses in February and March. After months off the bike, a half-day course with an advanced instructor is an excellent way to rebuild confidence and sharpen skills before the season proper. The Institute of Advanced Motorists (IAM) and RoSPA both offer motorcycle-specific programmes.

The MCN London motorcycle show usually falls in February — a great day out to see new bikes, gear, and get inspired for the year ahead. Ride there if conditions allow for the full experience.

Year in Review

December is a natural time to review your riding year. How many miles did you cover? Which tours were the highlights? What roads do you want to revisit? What new destinations are on the list for next year? Keeping a riding diary or photo log makes this review both enjoyable and useful for future planning.

The motorcycle press publishes yearend reviews and bike-of-the-year awards in December — good reading for winter evenings. If you're considering a new bike for 2027, December research and January test rides set you up for a spring purchase at the best prices.

Mental Preparation

Winter riding demands a different mindset from summer touring. Accept that distances will be shorter, conditions will be challenging, and comfort will be compromised. But also recognise that winter riding develops skills and resilience that make you a better rider year-round.

Set realistic expectations for winter rides. A 50-mile loop to a warm pub on a dry December day is a successful ride. Don't compare it to a 200-mile summer tour — they're different experiences with different rewards. The satisfaction of riding through winter, when most bikes are in garages, is its own unique pleasure.

Gift Ideas for Riders

December means Christmas shopping, and if you're buying for a motorcyclist (or dropping hints for your own list), touring-specific gifts are always welcome. Heated gloves, a quality neck tube, a tank bag, chain lube kits, and OS Maps subscriptions all make excellent presents. For the rider who has everything, an experience gift — a track day voucher, an advanced riding course, or a ferry booking for next summer's tour — creates anticipation through the winter months.

Motorcycle-themed books are perfect winter reading. Ted Simon's Jupiter's Travels, Robert Pirsig's Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance, and Sam Manicom's Into Africa are classics that fuel wanderlust from the comfort of an armchair. For UK-specific touring inspiration, look for route guidebooks covering Scotland, Wales, and England's national parks.

Route Planning for Winter

Winter routes should prioritise gritted main roads and avoid exposed mountain passes. The difference between a sheltered valley road and an exposed hilltop in winter can be 5-10 degrees Celsius and the difference between clear tarmac and black ice. Study your local council's gritting routes — these are the safest roads in cold weather.

Carry a phone with the What3Words app installed. If you break down in poor conditions on a remote winter road, being able to communicate your exact location to breakdown services is important when visibility is reduced and landmarks are obscured by weather. Read our UK Motorcycle Riding in May: Peak Spring Perfection guide for more.
keyTakeaways: February averages 3-8C with more frequent mild spells than January, though morning frost remains a hazard.
Daylight lengthens noticeably to roughly 7:15am sunrise and 5pm sunset by month's end.
Snowdrops carpet woodland floors, with the Cotswolds and Wye Valley particularly beautiful.
It is prime pre-season prep time: service the bike, check tyre pressures, lubricate the chain and treat salt corrosion.
IAM and RoSPA refresher courses and the MCN London show make February an ideal month to sharpen skills.

faq.q: Is February a good month to start riding again?
faq.a: February is a genuine transition month. Days are noticeably longer than January and milder spells appear more often, so dry, sunny riding days do occur. Roads still carry salt and grit and frost lingers in the morning, so time your rides for the warmest hours. Even a 20-minute dry-afternoon blast lifts the spirits after winter.

faq.q: What bike maintenance should I do in February?
faq.a: February is prime pre-season preparation time. Service the bike if it has been standing over winter, check tyre pressures because they drop in cold weather, lubricate the chain and check its tension, and charge the battery if the bike has been unused. Also clean and treat any salt corrosion left over from winter riding before the season proper begins.

faq.q: Where can I ride comfortably in February?
faq.a: Low-level routes in the south and west offer the mildest conditions. Coastal roads in Cornwall, Devon and Pembrokeshire can be surprisingly pleasant on a bright February day. Avoid mountain passes because snow and ice can persist at altitude right through the month. Keep expectations modest and enjoy the returning daylight.

faq.q: Are there any riding events in February?
faq.a: Yes. The MCN London motorcycle show usually falls in February and makes a great day out to see new bikes and gear. Many riding schools also run early-season refresher courses in February and March. A half-day with an advanced instructor from the IAM or RoSPA is an excellent way to rebuild confidence after months off the bike.

faq.q: Why are the days so important in February?
faq.a: The lengthening days are what make February feel hopeful. By the end of the month sunset reaches around 5pm, giving significantly more usable riding time than January's 4pm cut-off. Snowdrops appearing in woodland and the first longer-daylight rides are reliable signs that the riding season is becoming possible again.
